newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares rise on new government.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares rise on new government.

text.p: Indian shares jumped more than two percent on Monday after Inder Kumar Gujral was sworn in as India's new prime minister, defusing a political crisis that rocked financial markets.

"It's business as before," said Amit Prahladka, vice-president at Reliance Capital Asset Management Ltd. "The parties are virtually the same and there are unlikely to be any major changes in the cabinet."
Gujral retained the cabinet of his predecessor, H.D. Deve Gowda, except for Finance Minister P. Chidambaram and four other departing ministers.
Returning ministers will keep the same portfolios, and there was speculation that Chidambaram could be persuaded to return.
Officials said Gujral, who was sworn in on Monday at the head of a centre-left government backed by the Congress party, supported the pro-business budget proposed by Chidambaram.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index surged 103.27 points, or 2.8 percent, to close at 3799.79.
A 10 percent rally by Reliance Industries ahead of the company's annual results due on Tuesday also cheered market sentiment, traders said.
Stocks indices on the Bombay-based National Stock Exchange and on other regional bourses like Calcutta and Delhi rose by an average two percent.
"After the long uncertainty, there is some good news in the market," said Vijay Pandya, chief dealer at Classic Share & Stock Brokers.
Stock markets across the country were volatile during the crisis triggered by the Congress Party's decision last month to withdraw support from the ruling coalition.
Gujral told reporters after taking the oath of office that he would keep the foreign and finance ministry portfolios for himself in the new government.
Investors interpreted this as a sign that departing Finance Minister Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) might be persuaded to rejoin the new government.

The TMC, unhappy that its leader G.K. Moopanar was not chosen to lead Gujral's United Front, said on Saturday it would not join the government but would support the alliance from outside. But Gujral said he hoped the TMC would join his government.
"The fact that Gujral has kept the finance portfolio means he's still negotiating with TMC," said Keshav Sanghi, equities salesman at HSBC James Capel in Hong Kong.

"Hopefully, Gujral will manage to convince Moopanar to come back and you'll see some sort of compromise. The picture will will get a lot clearer once the vote of confidence and the budget go through," Sanghi said.
Gujral is due to face a vote of confidence in the lower house of parliament on Tuesday at 11 a.m. (0530 GMT).
Parliament is to take up budget proposals for the 1997/98 tax year starting in April after it reassembles on April 30.
"Temporarily, things seem to be settled," said the head of sales at a European brokerage. "We're recommending people stay invested and are asking them to stick to pivotals."
